newsitem.title: ITALY: Fresh scorn for Italian police escorts after death.
newsitem.headline: Fresh scorn for Italian police escorts after death.

text.p: High-speed armed police escorts, Italy's ultimate status symbol, were the target of fresh public outrage on Tuesday after a mother and her baby were killed in a crash with an armour-plated car that drove through a red light.
Maria Antonia Savona, 36, and her month-old son Riccardo died on Monday in the town of Trapani, western Sicily, on their way to visit the boy's grandmother.
They were passing a crossroads when an unmarked white armoured car carrying a magistrate in the Mafia-ridden area tore through a stop light with its siren wailing and ploughed into their vehicle.
Six people were injured in the smash, including the magistrate, Bernardo Petralia, his driver and two Carabinieri paramilitary police bodyguards.
"Escort car mows down mamma and child," the newspaper La Stampa said in a front-page headline. It and other newspapers questioned why the vehicle needed to jump the traffic light.

Armed police escorts for potential Mafia targets, cabinet ministers and other VIPs have long been under fire in Italy from a public whose contempt for displays of privilege was whetted by the country's huge political corruption scandals.
Interior Minister Giorgio Napolitano sought to respond to the popular mood last July when he announced a review by the new centre-left government of just who should be entitled to protection.
Napolitano was scathing about Monday's tragedy, saying his July notice had specifically ordered escort cars to stick to speed limits and obey traffic regulations.
"We have got to put a stop to inadmissible behaviour in the way vehicles carrying people protected for security reasons are driven," Napolitano said in a statement.
Raffaele Costa, an opposition centre-right politician, said: "It is unthinkable that innocent victims are continuing to pay, often with their life, the price of arrogance and privilege."

Vehicles on Italy's crowded city streets frequently have to pull into the kerbside or mount pavements at the sound of approaching sirens as official cars roar down the road with policemen hanging out of their windows waving "stop" batons.
Romans this week have watched in awe at passage through the Italian capital of a 16-vehicle motorcade that accompanies visiting Cuban President Fidel Castro wherever he goes.
The convoy includes four Maseratis and a four-wheel-drive with a light machinegun poking through the sunroof.
La Stampa newspaper quoted one unnamed official driver as saying he doubted much could be done to slow down.

"You can find yourself in the centre of Rome with 20 minutes to get to the airport. Of course you take risks," the daily quoted him as saying. The normal journey takes about 40 minutes in regular traffic.
